opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a really interesting contrast, and I think it tells us something about what these models are actually doing.

If you give a large language model one of those odd everyday scenarios, say someone walking into a kitchen and finding the fridge door open and a trail of water across the floor, and you ask it what might have happened, it's often remarkably good. It'll come up with plausible explanations: the freezer has defrosted, someone left the door ajar, maybe the dog got in. That's a kind of commonsense, abductive reasoning, and for a long time in AI it was one of the hardest things to capture. In the old symbolic days we tried to hand-code that sort of knowledge, and it was a nightmare. The frame problem and so on. So it's genuinely striking that these models do it so fluently. They've absorbed an enormous amount of the background knowledge that humans bring to everyday situations, simply by being trained on the vast record of how people talk about the world.

Multi-step problems are a different matter. If you have to chain together many inferences, keep track of intermediate states, and not lose the thread, that's where the cracks tend to show, at least in the base models. Each step might look locally plausible, but errors compound, and the model can drift off somewhere that doesn't hold together. Now, things like chain-of-thought prompting, and more recently models trained specifically to reason at length before answering, have improved this a lot. But I'd still say there's an asymmetry. The everyday stuff plays to their strengths, which is a kind of broad, associative, pattern-rich knowledge. The long, rigorous chains need something more like systematic, step-by-step control, and that's something they've had to be coaxed or trained into.

I'd add a word of caution about how we interpret all this, though. It's very tempting to look at the commonsense performance and say "it understands the situation" in just the way we do. I think we should be careful with that kind of language. These are very exotic entities, and what's going on under the hood may be quite unlike human understanding, even when the outputs look humanlike. Equally, when they fail at multi-step reasoning, it doesn't mean there's nothing there. So I try to steer between the two extremes: not dismissing them as mere stochastic parrots, but not over-anthropomorphising them either. The interesting scientific work is in characterising precisely what kind of competence this is.

r001.rationale: It says models are often remarkably good at offering plausible explanations for odd everyday scenarios.

r002.rationale: It says multistep problems challenge models, but does not state that these are problems humans struggle with.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's an interesting distinction, and I think it's worth being careful about what we mean by each of those things. If you give one of these models an odd little vignette — someone walks into a kitchen, finds the fridge door open and a wet patch on the floor, and you ask what happened — they're often remarkably good at producing a plausible account. And I think that's not so surprising, actually, because that's exactly the kind of thing that's saturated in the training data. Human beings spend an enormous amount of their lives explaining mundane situations to each other, and so the statistical regularities that underpin that sort of commonsense explanation are very richly represented. The model has, in effect, absorbed a huge amount of folk physics and folk psychology, and it can deploy that quite fluently.

Now, the thing I'd caution against is sliding from that observation to the claim that the model has a model of the world in the sense that you or I do. I'm agnostic about that, really. What we can say is that it produces the kind of text that a person with a world model would produce. Whether there's something underlying it that deserves the name "understanding" is a much harder question, and I think our ordinary language starts to creak when we apply it to these systems.

The multi-step problems are a different story, and I think they expose something important. When you ask a model to carry out a long chain of reasoning — a planning problem, say, or a mathematical argument with many dependent steps — the errors tend to compound. Each step might be individually quite likely to be right, but if there's a small probability of going astray at every point, then over twenty or thirty steps that adds up. And crucially, the model doesn't, by default, have a mechanism for checking itself against reality. A human doing a long calculation can stop, look back, verify an intermediate result. The base model is just generating the next token.

Of course, there are ways to ameliorate that. Chain-of-thought prompting, scratchpads, getting the model to externalise its intermediate steps, or embedding the model in a larger system that gives it tools and the ability to iterate. And those help a great deal. But I think it's telling that we need those scaffolds. It suggests the kind of competence being displayed in the everyday case and the kind required for extended reasoning aren't quite the same thing, even if they emerge from the same underlying mechanism.

So my assessment would be: very good at the former, in a way that's genuinely impressive and that I wouldn't have predicted a decade ago, and considerably more brittle at the latter — though improving, and improving in part because people are building the right architectures around them. What I'd resist is the temptation to read too much into either side. The fluency on everyday cases shouldn't be over-interpreted as deep understanding, and the fragility on long problems shouldn't be dismissed as a mere engineering detail, because it tells us something about the nature of what these systems are doing.

r001.rationale: The response says models are “remarkably good” at producing plausible accounts of odd everyday vignettes.

r002.rationale: It describes long, complex reasoning tasks as brittle for models, but does not state that these are problems humans struggle with.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an interesting distinction there. If you describe an odd everyday situation, a large language model can often produce a very plausible explanation. That’s quite striking, because it may require bringing together several pieces of commonsense knowledge that we wouldn’t ordinarily think to spell out. But producing a plausible explanation isn’t quite the same thing as establishing what actually happened. There may be several explanations compatible with the description.

When you move to a problem that requires many steps, the challenge is different. Each step has to be correct, and the model has to keep track of the consequences of earlier steps. A small mistake can send the whole thing off course, even if every subsequent sentence sounds perfectly reasonable. So I wouldn’t infer from a really impressive answer to an everyday puzzle that the model necessarily has a reliable capacity for extended reasoning. We have to look quite carefully at the particular task and at how robust the performance is.

r001.rationale: It says models can often produce plausible explanations for odd everyday situations.

r002.rationale: It explains why multistep problems challenge models, but does not say that these are problems humans struggle with too.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a rather striking contrast. If you describe some slightly odd everyday situation and ask a language model to explain what might have happened, it can often come up with a very plausible explanation. That’s impressive, because it seems to draw on quite a broad understanding of how the world works, what people want, and how they behave.

But that doesn’t necessarily translate into being able to solve a problem that requires a long sequence of reasoning steps. You might get each individual step right much of the time, but a small error early on can send the whole thing off course. And the model may carry on producing a very fluent explanation without noticing that it’s made a mistake.

So I’d distinguish that ability to make a good, context-sensitive inference from the ability to sustain reliable reasoning over many steps. The first can be remarkably good while the second is still quite fragile.

r001.rationale: It says models can often give a plausible explanation for a slightly odd everyday situation.

r002.rationale: It says long sequences of reasoning can be fragile for models, but does not state that these are problems humans struggle with too.
